title: Professional Cloud Documentation
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of professional cloud documentation and its relationship to Optional Specializations and Professional Skills.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to professional cloud documentation.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn professional cloud documentation in the context of Optional Specializations and Professional Skills. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Professional Cloud Documentation matters because it is one part of professional paths and specialist skills. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Module 24: Optional Specializations and Professional Skills
content_blocks.alt_text: Five-step overview for module 24, Optional Specializations and Professional Skills, followed by verification, least-privilege security, recovery, and cost-cleanup checks.
content_blocks.caption: Module 24 learning sequence: understand the concept, make a controlled design/configuration, verify behavior, and document security/reliability/cost trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Professional Cloud Documentation belongs to Optional Specializations and Professional Skills. Use specialist paths to go deeper after the shared core. Professional evidence includes repeatable projects, diagrams, runbooks, test records, cost reviews and documentation—not course completion alone.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Technical architecture documents; Operational runbooks; Disaster recovery plans; Security and cost review reports. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For professional cloud documentation, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Technical architecture documents
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: Operational runbooks
items.text: Compare the available option with the workload requirement; record the operational, security, availability and cost trade-offs rather than assuming one option is always best.

items.title: Disaster recovery plans
items.text: Define the failure scenario and recovery objective, then test detection, recovery, data consistency and rollback. Treat recovery evidence as a deliverable, not an assumption.

items.title: Security and cost review reports
items.text: Estimate the complete workload, including requests, storage, data transfer and dependent services. Compare the estimate with actual usage and alerts; an alert is not a hard spend cap.

content_blocks.title: Professional cloud documentation package
content_blocks.code: Architecture diagram + decision records + infrastructure templates + test evidence + monitoring/runbook + recovery proof + cost estimate
content_blocks.expected_output: Treat this package as a reviewable artifact; screenshots alone do not prove correctness, security or recovery.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This block is an inspectable example, not an AWS action performed by CodeLeaf. Review the example as text and adapt it only after checking current official service documentation. Do not apply/deploy changes in a real account without account-owner approval, least-privilege permissions and a reviewed cost/cleanup plan.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “Professional Cloud Documentation”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for Professional Cloud Documentation with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: Professional Cloud Documentation is taught as part of Optional Specializations and Professional Skills.

Use specialist paths to go deeper after the shared core. Professional evidence includes repeatable projects, diagrams, runbooks, test records, cost reviews and documentation—not course completion alone.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
